rewritten_text:
Knights and horses wearing heavy armor couldn't move very quickly. These men would travel as fast as they could, and with the ground now firm and free of snow or mud, they would probably manage seven miles an hour. They would need to change horses twice and should arrive around six, or shortly afterward. There would still be plenty of daylight. They would spot the white cloth I intended to tie around my right arm, and I would take command. We would surround the prison and free the king in no time. Considering everything, it would be a colorful, impressive spectacle, though I would have preferred noon for its greater theatrical effect.

Meanwhile, to give myself another option, I thought I would find some of the people I had recognized earlier and reveal who I was. That could get us out of trouble without waiting for the knights. But it was a dangerous business, and I had to proceed carefully. I needed magnificent clothes, and I couldn't simply rush off and put them on. No, I would have to work up to them gradually, buying one outfit after another from shops well apart, each a little finer than the last, until I reached silk and velvet and was ready to carry out my plan. So I set off.

But the scheme collapsed in a flash! At the very first corner, I ran straight into one of our slaves, prowling around with a watchman. Just then I coughed, and he shot me a look that pierced me to the marrow. I suppose he thought he'd heard that cough before. I immediately ducked into a shop and moved along the counter, asking prices while watching from the corner of my eye. The two men had stopped and were talking together, looking through the doorway. I decided to escape through the back, if there was a way out. I asked the shopwoman whether I could step outside there to search for the escaped slave, who was believed to be hiding somewhere behind the building. I explained that I was an officer in disguise, and that my partner was at the door with one of the murderers in custody. Would she kindly tell him not to wait, but to go immediately to the far end of the back alley, ready to intercept the fugitive when I flushed him out?

Burning with excitement at the chance to see one of those already famous murderers, she went to deliver the message at once.

“Then listen! You!” Monks replied. “When his father fell ill in Rome, his wife—my mother, from whom he'd long been separated—traveled from Paris to join him and took me along. For all I know, she went to look after his property, since she had little affection for him and he had little for her. He didn't recognize us. He'd lost consciousness and slept until the following day, when he died. Among the papers in his desk were two dated the night his illness began and addressed to you”—he turned to Mr. Brownlow—“enclosed with a short note for you. On the outside of the package were instructions that it wasn't to be sent until after his death. One document was a letter to that girl Agnes; the other was a will.”

“What did the letter say?” asked Mr. Brownlow.

“The letter? A sheet covered with writing crisscrossed over itself, full of remorseful confessions and prayers for God to help her. He'd fed the girl a story about some mysterious secret, which he'd explain one day, that prevented him from marrying her just then. So she'd kept patiently trusting him, until she trusted too much and lost what no one could ever restore. At that point, she was only a few months from giving birth. He explained everything he'd intended to do to conceal her disgrace if he lived. If he died, he begged her not to curse his memory or believe that she or their child would be punished for their sin, because all the guilt was his. He reminded her of the day he'd given her the little locket and the ring engraved with her first name, leaving a space for the surname he hoped to give her someday. He begged her to keep it and wear it against her heart as before. Then he rambled on wildly, repeating the same words again and again, as though he'd lost his mind. I believe he had.”

“The will,” said Mr. Brownlow, as Oliver's tears flowed freely.

Monks said nothing.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow continued for him, “expressed the same feelings as the letter. He described the misery his wife had caused him, and the rebelliousness, depravity, malice, and prematurely vicious passions of you, his only son, who had been taught to hate him. He left you and your mother an annual income of eight hundred pounds each. He divided the greater part of his estate equally between Agnes Fleming and their child, provided the child was born alive and lived to come of age.

“I trust I shall shortly have the pleasure of presenting my son to you,” said Mr. Weston.

Mrs. Elton, quite prepared to interpret this hope as a special compliment to herself, bestowed a most gracious smile.

“You have, I suppose, heard of a certain Frank Churchill,” he went on, “and are aware that he is my son, although his name is not mine.”

“Oh, certainly, and I shall be delighted to make his acquaintance. Mr. Elton, I am sure, will call upon him without delay, and we shall both be most happy to welcome him to the Vicarage.”

“That is very kind of you. Frank will be delighted, I am certain. He is expected in town next week, perhaps earlier. A letter received to-day informs us of it. I encountered the letters on my way this morning and, recognizing my son's handwriting, took the liberty of opening his—although addressed not to me but to Mrs. Weston. She is his chief correspondent, I assure you. A letter to me is quite a rarity.”

“So you actually opened a letter meant for her! Oh, Mr. Weston”—with an affected laugh—“I must object to that. What a dangerous precedent! Pray do not permit your neighbours to copy you. Upon my word, if this is what awaits me, we married women must make a stand! Oh, Mr. Weston, I would never have thought it of you!”

“Yes, we men are dreadful creatures. You must look after yourself, Mrs. Elton. This letter says—it is very brief, dashed off merely to inform us—that they are all coming directly to town because of Mrs. Churchill. She has been unwell throughout the winter and finds Enscombe too cold, so they are to travel south without a moment's delay.”

“Really! From Yorkshire, I believe? Is not Enscombe in Yorkshire?”

“Yes, some hundred and ninety miles from London—a substantial journey.”

“Yes, indeed, very substantial. Sixty-five miles more than the journey from Maple Grove to London. Yet what does distance signify, Mr. Weston, to people with great fortunes? You would be astonished by the way my brother, Mr. Suckling, sometimes flies about. You will scarcely credit it, but twice in a single week he and Mr. Bragge traveled to London and back with four horses.”

“The difficulty with the distance from Enscombe,” Mr. Weston said, “is that Mrs. Churchill, as we understand matters, has been unable to rise from her sofa for an entire week. In his last letter, Frank said she complained of being too weak to reach her conservatory without taking both his arm and his uncle's!”
